chunks: From him, from several of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Asbat, who said: My father informed me, saying:

I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and a man said to him: 'I have wind in my belly (bloating), and drinking nabidh suits me.' He said: 'What is your matter with what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden?' He said that three times. 'Stick to this maris, which you grind at night and drink in the morning, and grind in the morning and drink in the evening.' He said: 'This causes bloating in my belly.' He said: 'Shall I guide you to what is more beneficial than this? Stick to supplication, for it is a cure for every disease.'
We said to him: 'Is its little and much forbidden?' He said: 'Yes. Its little and much is forbidden.'

key_terms.النَّبِيذ: Nabidh (fermented drink, typically of dates or raisins in water)
key_terms.الْمَرِيس: Al-Maris (a specific type of preparation or drink mentioned in the context)
key_terms.قَلِيلُهُ وَ كَثِيرُهُ: Its little and much (indicating the ruling applies regardless of quantity)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on nabidh in Shia jurisprudence according to hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic principle of 'kathir wa qalil' (much and little) regarding nabidh, where the Imam clarifies that even small quantities are prohibited, countering the notion that minor amounts are permissible for medicinal use. It highlights the transition from physical remedies to spiritual ones, as the Imam recommends supplication (dua) as a universal cure, reflecting the Shia emphasis on the interplay between physical health and divine grace.
